news.title: [SMM Analysis] Lithium Carbonate Market in Deficit in Q3 2026: Why Prices Failed to Rise？In Q3 2026, China's lithium carbonate market saw a weak trend with the price center moving lower month by month. Alongside the persistently weakening prices, the supply-demand balance was negative for three consecutive months. The deficit moving in the opposite direction of prices was the most noteworthy phenomenon of the quarter. Prices did not fall sharply in a one-way move, but instead declined stepwise on a monthly basis: a stalemate between upstream and downstream in July, narrow consolidation in August, and a marked acceleration of the decline in September, with month-end spot prices having pulled back nearly 40% from the year's high in mid-May. I. Price Path: From Two-Way Tug-of-War to One-Way Decline The market was in a stalemate in July. Downstream players bought the dip below the 150,000 yuan/mt level but showed little willingness to chase prices above 160,000 yuan/mt; upstream held quotes firm with limited room for concessions. The psychological price spread between the two sides persisted throughout the quarter, with transactions concentrated at the lower end of the price range and the average price pulling back slightly MoM. In August, some lithium chemical plants resumed production after maintenance, while upstream continued to hold prices firm and downstream maintained purchasing as needed. The phased mismatch was not resolved, and the market entered consolidation, with the MoM decline in the average price narrowing to within 2%. The pattern changed in September: production resumptions after maintenance drove output higher, transactions slowed rapidly after pre-holiday stockpiling ended, the driver of concentrated buying disappeared, and the one-way downward shift in the price center was confirmed, with the monthly decline widening notably. II. Supply: The Mismatch Between Maintenance and Production Resumptions The pace of supply in Q3 corresponded closely with the pace of prices. In July, some smelters on both the spodumene and lepidolite routes underwent concentrated maintenance, with production falling nearly 10% MoM, which became the main factor supporting prices. From August onward, production resumptions after maintenance proceeded one after another, salt lakes entered their seasonal peak production period, port arrivals of spodumene increased, and production rebounded MoM; September saw further slight growth. During the same period, production restrictions at salt lakes, maintenance shutdowns in the recycling segment, and raw material constraints on lithium extraction from slag utilization formed offsets, limiting the extent of the supply recovery—supply elasticity was restored, but growth did not get out of control. The implication of this pace is that the tightness in July was at the production schedule level, not the resource level. The market already had expectations for the production resumption timetable, so when production rebounded as scheduled in August and September, prices did not receive effective support. Instead, the realization of expectations removed the upside potential. III. Demand: The source of growth has shifted The demand side showed clear divergence across levels. Throughout the quarter, cathode material and battery cell production continued to grow QoQ, with cumulative growth in the battery cell segment exceeding 20%; NEV sales, however, declined MoM twice in July and September, with cumulative quarterly decline of nearly 10%. This means the growth in lithium demand in Q3 was no longer primarily driven by the vehicle segment. This structural shift in demand has direct implications for lithium carbonate: the cathode routes corresponding to energy storage and export orders are dominated by LFP, whose raw material is precisely lithium carbonate. This also provides a structural explanation for why the decline in lithium carbonate prices was smaller than what NEV sales would suggest—the center of demand is shifting from passenger vehicles to power-side energy storage projects. The divergence in demand also explains purchasing behavior. Cathode and battery cell enterprises maintained production amid moderate order visibility, but refused to build raw material inventory amid expectations of falling prices, creating a combination of "rising production, cautious purchasing." IV. Policy: Costs shift from implicit to explicit On July 17, three government departments issued a notice imposing a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries effective September 1, at a rate of 2%, rising to 4% from September 2027, covering production, commissioned processing, and import/export stages. Three details in the policy design determine its market impact: complete energy storage systems are tax-exempt; battery cells assembled into battery clusters are taxable but deductible; exports are taxed first and refunded later, with the refund rate reduced from 9% to 6%. The significance of the policy for Q3 market conditions lies not in the tax rate itself, but in the shift of the tax burden on battery cells and battery clusters from implicit to explicit. Explicit costs can be passed through; implicit costs can only be absorbed. In the short term, the implementation of the tax burden compressed profit margins in the battery cell and battery cluster segments, reinforcing downstream purchasing as needed and pushing for lower prices; the acceleration of the price decline in September coincided with the September 1 implementation date. In the medium term, the explicit tax burden will accelerate the exit of inefficient capacity, which directionally helps raise the cost curve, but this effect is not reflected in Q3 prices. Meanwhile, Shandong Document No. 632 removed the pre-approval constraint on grid connection for new wind and solar power projects with energy storage allocation, allowing enterprises to independently determine the scale, duration, and technology route of energy storage allocation. For operational PV and wind power projects included in the plan, the energy storage allocation caps are 50% and 30% of installed capacity, respectively, with unified dispatch, metering, settlement, and participation in the spot market. The shift from mandatory energy storage allocation to economic-driven deployment means short-term lithium demand growth depends more on spot revenue, weakening the floor effect. V. Inventory: The Extent and Structure of Destocking Inventory changes provide direct evidence of demand divergence. During the thirteen weeks from early July to early October, inventories across major segments fell by more than 30% in aggregate. The structural differences are even more noteworthy: downstream cathode plant inventories were nearly halved, smelter inventories fell by nearly 40%, while trader inventories pulled back only slightly, with their share of total inventory rising from under 30% to over one-third. The destocking was concentrated downstream, indicating that Q3 inventory changes were driven by the consumption side rather than proactive destocking on the production side. Upstream players completed shipments through long-term contract deliveries and holding back from selling, while cathode plants ran their raw material inventories down to relatively low levels. September purchases included some pre-holiday restocking at low prices, but trading quickly turned thin once stockpiling ended. The decline in absolute inventory levels and the shift in structure occurred simultaneously: as total volume decreased, inventory holdings tilted from industrial segments toward trading segments. The implications of this shift for prices differ from those of the change in total volume—industrial inventory will be consumed, whereas trading inventory tends to be released when prices rebound. The same quantity, held by different parties, does not act on prices in the same direction. VI. The Divergence Between Deficits and Prices The Q3 supply-demand balance was negative for three consecutive months, with a cumulative quarterly deficit of approximately 84,000 mt LCE; correspondingly, the price center moved lower month by month. The deficit and prices moving in opposite directions is key to understanding this quarter's market. The two can be reconciled in the data. Over the same period, inventory destocking amounted to approximately 68,000 mt, on the same order of magnitude as the quarterly deficit—the deficit was largely filled by inventory rather than cleared through prices. Inventory served as a buffer, allowing prices to continue falling despite the existence of a deficit. This is the first explanation for the coexistence of a deficit and falling prices. The second explanation lies in the time dimension of pricing. What the market traded in Q3 was not the spot tightness from July to September, but rather the supply recovery after production resumptions and expectations of more distant supply growth. When the path of supply recovery is clear and the timetable is predictable, the support that a current-period deficit provides to prices is significantly weakened; the production rebound in August and September merely realized expectations that had already been priced in during July. The third explanation lies in the structure of participation. The rising share of inventory held by trading segments means that more inventory is now held for price trading rather than production turnover; at the same time, the futures market has become the primary venue for price discovery, and industrial enterprises hedge forward production during price rises, meaning rebounds may face sustained selling pressure. The change in holding structure has altered the direction in which the same quantity of inventory acts on prices. VII. Conclusion Overall, the Q3 2026 lithium carbonate market can be summarized as follows: the recovery of supply elasticity, the explicit pass-through of policy costs, and the migration of inventory toward the trade segment combined to drive the price center lower month by month. Prices during the quarter exhibited two characteristics: first, the decline unfolded in a stepwise manner, with intra-month momentum exceeding monthly averages; second, the deficit diverged from the price direction, with inventory serving as the primary buffer. For the quarter itself, the market completed an adjustment of "expectations leading, inventory lagging": prices reflected production resumptions and policy costs ahead of time, while inventory completed its shift to the trade segment at quarter-end. This combination was both the outcome of Q3 market dynamics and the starting point for Q4.Nov 16, 2026 17:04 (GMT+8)
